For C=A(M,K)B(K,N), useful arithmetic is 2MKN FLOPs. A simple lower bound for one-device HBM traffic is element_bytes·(MK+KN+MN), assuming each input is read once and output written once; actual tiling, reuse, accumulation, and dtype conversions can increase traffic. Arithmetic intensity is FLOPs divided by bytes, and the roofline is min(peak_FLOPs, bandwidth·intensity).

Specify the shard layout before estimating communication. Row-shard A/C with replicated B requires each device to hold B, while sharding the reduction dimension K creates partial outputs that need reduction. Include per-collective startup latency, communicated bytes, topology, overlap, and the number of concurrent transfers; a bandwidth-only number is not enough. Model compute, HBM, and network bounds for the local shard separately.

For example, a square 8192 matrix multiply uses about 1.10e12 FLOPs. At two-byte storage the ideal three-matrix traffic is about 403 MB, yielding roughly 2731 FLOPs/byte before communication. Divide local work by achievable throughput, not peak marketing throughput, and add any unhidden collective time. Validate with a small benchmark; launch overhead, imbalance, and memory capacity can invalidate the idealized bound.

**Mathematical and practical explanation.** For square matrices of size n with two-byte storage and ideal single reads/writes, intensity is $2n^3/(6n^2)=n/3$ FLOPs per byte. The roofline lower-bound time is $\max(F/P,BW_{bytes}/BW_{rate})$ before unhidden communication and overhead. Actual performance needs measured achievable rates and the specified distributed shard layout. [3](https://jax-ml.github.io/scaling-book/)

For the implementation or system context discussed above, see [1](https://jax-ml.github.io/scaling-book/sharding/) and [2](https://jax-ml.github.io/scaling-book/roofline/).
